pages.p:
In unit 8 you made objects by hand. But what if you need 100 similar objects, like 100 players in a game? Writing each one is slow.

A **class** is a blueprint. You write it once. Then you use «new» to build objects from it. Each object built from a class is called an **instance**.
pages.tip: Class names start with a capital letter: «Dog», not «dog». The word «new» builds a fresh object.

pages.p:
The **constructor** is a special method. JavaScript runs it automatically each time you write «new». Use it to give the new object its starting data.

Inside it, «this» means the new object that is being built. So «this.name = name» stores the value in the object.
pages.tip: The arguments you give to «new Dog(...)» go straight into the constructor's parameters.

pages.p:
Functions inside a class are called **methods**. You write them without the word «function». Do not put commas between them.

Inside a method, «this» means the object that called the method. To read or change the object's data, you must write «this.count», not just «count».
pages.tip: Methods are written one after another, with no commas between them.

pages.p: Each instance has its own data. Changing one object does not change the others. All of them share the same methods, so you write the code only once.
pages.tip: A short method can fit on one line. Both styles are fine.

pages.p: A method can call another method of the same object. Use «this» again: «this.canBuy(price)». Methods can also «return» a value, just like normal functions.
pages.tip: The second «buy(6)» fails: only 4 coins are left.

pages.p:
A **getter** looks like a property, but it runs code. Write «get» before the method name. When you use it, you do **not** write brackets.

Getters are great for values that come from other data, like an area. The value is always fresh.
pages.tip: Write «r.area», not «r.area()». With brackets you get an error, because «area» is not a function.

pages.p:
A **static** method belongs to the class itself, not to its instances. You call it on the class name. Use it for helpers that do not need one particular object.

You already know some: «Math.round» and «Object.keys» are static methods.
pages.tip: An instance does not get static methods. «u.unit» does not exist, only «Circle.unit» does.

pages.p:
Sometimes one class is a special kind of another. A cat is an animal. Write «class Cat extends Animal» and Cat gets everything Animal has, plus its own new methods.

The class you extend is the **parent**. The new class is the **child**.
pages.o:
Tom makes a sound.
Tom says meow.
pages.tip: Cat has no constructor of its own, so it uses the parent's constructor.

pages.p:
If the child needs its own constructor, it must call «super(...)» first. «super» runs the parent's constructor. Only after that can you use «this».

If you use «this» before «super()», JavaScript gives an error.
pages.tip: Rule: in a child constructor, write «super(...)» on the first line.

pages.p:
A child can write a method with the **same name** as the parent's. The child's version wins. This is called **overriding**.

Inside it, «super.speak()» still calls the parent's version, if you want both.
pages.tip: You can use «new Cow()» straight away and call a method on it in the same line.

pages.p:
«x instanceof Y» is «true» when «x» was built from class «Y», or from any class that extends «Y». Otherwise it is «false».

So a Cat is a Cat, and it is also an Animal. But it is not a Dog.
pages.tip: An empty class body «{}» is allowed. It is useful for short examples.

hand.q: What does the word «new» do in «new Dog()»?
hand.ans: It builds an object and runs its constructor
wrong: It copies the whole Dog class into a new variable
It deletes the old Dog object from memory
It only checks that the class Dog exists
hand.why: «new» creates a fresh instance, runs the constructor, and gives you the object back.

hand.q: Complete the special method that sets up a new object.
hand.why: The method that runs automatically with «new» must be called «constructor».
The count starts at 0 and each call to «add» makes it 1 bigger. Three calls give 3.

hand.q: Inside a method, why do we write «this.name» and not just «name»?
hand.ans: «name» alone would be a different variable
wrong: «name» alone is much slower than «this.name» is
«this» is a required comment before every variable
«name» only works inside the constructor method
hand.why: Data of the object lives in «this». A bare «name» would look for a normal variable, and there is none, so you get an error.
Every instance has its own data. Making «b» does not change «a».

hand.q: Put the lines in order to build and print one car.
hand.why: First write the class (the blueprint), then build an instance with «new», then use it.
A getter is read like a property. «sq.area» runs the getter and returns 5 * 5.
The word «get» before the method name turns it into a getter, which you read without brackets.

hand.q: How do you call a static method «make» of the class «Robot»?
hand.why: A static method belongs to the class, so you call it on the class name. Instances do not have it.
«Circle.unit()» builds a circle with radius 1. Its «r» is 1, and 1 + 4 is 5.
«Dog» extends «Animal», so it inherits the constructor and the «hello» method.
«super(name)» runs the parent's constructor. It must come before «this» is used.
A Dog is built from a class that extends Animal, so «instanceof Animal» is true too.

hard.why: «a» gets 2, then «b» gets 5. Then «a.add(b.n)» adds 5 to «a», so a is 7. «b» stays 5.
«C.say» first calls «B.say», which first calls «A.say». The text grows from A to AB to ABC.
Default parameters work in constructors. A missing argument and an explicit «undefined» both use the default.
The areas are 6, 20 and 1. The reduce adds them: 6 + 20 + 1 = 27.

hard.q: A getter «area» exists in a class. What happens with «console.log(r.area())»?
hard.ans: It throws a TypeError: a number is not a function
wrong: It prints the area, because brackets are optional
It prints «undefined» because the getter is hidden
It prints the source text of the getter code
hard.why: A getter is read like a property. Its value is already a number, so adding «()» tries to call a number.
A Puppy counts as a Dog and as an Animal. But a plain Animal is not a Dog: the parent is not an instance of its child.
The constructor can use normal code. The ternary turns the negative age into 0, and the text joins as «Lee0».

hard.q: A child class has its own constructor, but never calls «super()» and uses «this.x = 1». What happens on «new Child()»?
hard.ans: It throws an error: «super()» must come first
wrong: It works, and the parent's data is copied automatically
It works, but only the child's own data exists
hard.why: A child with its own constructor must call «super()» before it touches «this». Without it you get a ReferenceError.
The static method builds a Temp with 100 Celsius. The getter converts it back: 100 * 9 / 5 + 32 is 212.
«hi» comes from A, but «this» is a B object. So «this.num()» finds B's version, which gives "2".

items.symptom: It crashes with: ReferenceError: count is not defined.
items.why: The data lives on the object. Inside a method you must write «this.count»; plain «count» is a variable that does not exist.

items.symptom: It crashes with: Class constructor Dog cannot be invoked without 'new'.
items.why: A class is not a normal function. You must write «new» to build an instance.

items.symptom: It crashes with: TypeError: r.area is not a function. It should print 12.
items.why: A getter is read like a property, without brackets. «r.area» is already the number 12.

items.symptom: It prints undefined, but it should print Rex.
items.why: «super()» calls the parent constructor. Without «name» inside the brackets, the parent stores undefined.

items.symptom: It crashes with: TypeError: d.bark is not a function.
items.why: A static method belongs to the class, not to its instances. A method that uses the object's data must not be static.

items.symptom: It prints undefined, but it should print Moo.
items.why: The method has curly braces but no «return», so it gives back undefined.

project.title: Bank Account
project.brief:
Write a function «bankBalance(start, actions)». «start» is the money in the account at the beginning. «actions» is an array of steps. Each step is an array like «["deposit", 50]» or «["withdraw", 30]».

The starter already has an «Account» class. Finish its two methods:
- «deposit(amount)» adds the amount, but only if the amount is more than 0.
- «withdraw(amount)» takes the amount away, but only if the account has enough money. Otherwise it does nothing.

Then make «bankBalance» build an account, run every action in order, and return the final balance.

Example: «bankBalance(100, [["deposit", 50], ["withdraw", 30]])» is 120.
